There's a hollow in the pedestal where I keep one nugget, the Kind Nugget. Whoever gets junk three times running leaves with it. Nobody knows that. Now you do.
Here's the real secret of the ring: there isn't one. I've sung to it, cursed it, held the ingot upside down. Gold gives what it gives. Keep that from the Hold.
No gold on you and still at my ring? Then stand back and watch the others. Learn the shouting. Friends don't pay for lessons.

lines: My first time at the ring I dropped the ingot. It rolled all the way round the circle while the Hold watched. I've never dropped one since. Practice is being embarrassed once.

lines.text: Go on, make a wish before I take your gold. A wish helps the gold decide. Probably.

replies.text: Ha! Everyone wants the fire potion. Wish for something smaller and you might get it. Wish big and the ring laughs.
THAT is the right answer. Gold loves a trusting fool. Hold out the ingot.
Then you'll get junk and you'll be right. Sad way to win, that.

lines.text: Think you could run a ring? Answer fast. The gold is listening.

replies.text: Easily! Ha! Loud and sure. That's half of it. The other half is not minding when the ring laughs at you.
Everyone does. The trick is to shout WITH a plan. Mine is the loudest plan in the Hold.

lines: Haggling is three things: loud, slow and sad. Loud to start. Slow so they worry. Sad at the end, so they feel bad and add something.
Never name a price first. The first to say a number loses a nugget. Oldest rule in the Hold, and the only one nobody argues about.
Watch their eyes, not their purse. A Piglin staring at your gold is already yours. One staring at the exit is already gone.
A good haggle ends with both of you shouting and both of you happy. If only one of you is shouting, somebody's being robbed. Make sure it's them.
Turn your back halfway through. Make a show of leaving. Nine in ten come running. The tenth gets a nugget thrown at his head. Ha!
Praise their helmet. Praise it a lot. Then ask for a better price. A Piglin can't say no to someone who loves his helmet.
Never haggle hungry. A hungry Bartermaster agrees to anything that comes with a roast. I once sold my own stool for one rib.
Never count your take where the buyer can hear. It tells him how much you've got and how jealous to be.
Wanderers are the worst to haggle with. They've seen every Hold's prices. One 'it's cheaper in the next Hold' can wreck a hundred of my deals.
The Magmari haggle worse than anyone. They never stop. Not when they win, not when they lose, not when they leave. I once heard one haggle with a chain.

lines.text: My teacher, Mawgra Loud-Lung, called haggling a fight with no blood. I said then I want blood. She said that's why I'd stay at the ring forever. She was right. I'm still cross.
Mawgra once talked a Magmari into paying double for his own chain. He thanked her. She never got over it. Neither did he, I hope.
The real secret of haggling is that you must like them. Truly. Even the stingy ones. Once I like a Piglin I can only cheat him a little, and he feels it, and he comes back.
When I'm tired I let the buyer win. A small win, just enough to leave grinning. A grin is worth a hundred haggles. A grin comes back with friends.

lines: When I'm losing I haggle in rhymes. Nobody can stay angry at a rhyme. 'Nugget, nugget, give me ten, I'll be back to haggle again.' Awful. Works.

lines.text: Test time. I want your best helmet for two nuggets. Go.

replies.text: TEN?! Wonderful. Ridiculous. Now you're haggling. We'll settle at three. Maybe four. Get out.
Fine?! You never say fine first! Where's your spine? Try again. Louder.
Bad! Ha! Good move, insult the goods. Wrong helmet, though. That one's mine. Now we're even.

lines.text: So tell me, gold-wearer. Do you haggle, or do you just pay?

replies.text: Then you and I will argue until the lava cools. Wonderful. I'll bring snacks.
Just pay! Ha! The best buyer in the Nether and the worst haggler. Stay close.

lines: Wind first. A hoglin smells you from three trees away. So you walk with the wind in your face. If the wind turns, you turn. If you can't turn, you go home. Pride is for the Hold, not the hunt.
Load the crossbow before you enter the trees. Not after. After is when you're looking at a tusk.
You find the rooting first: torn fungus, churned ground, a smell like wet leather. Then the dung. Then the hoglin. The dung is the happy sign.
Quiet feet are learned on old bridges, over the lava, where one loud step means a long fall. Hold-raised hunters learn it slow. I fell twice.
A charging hoglin is faster than you but can't turn. So you step aside at the last breath. Step too early and it turns. Step too late and you're a story.
Hunting a sleeper gets you meat. Hunting a charger gets you a story. I like a story with my meat.
One bolt for the leg, one for the flank, the third for the shouting. The shouting is the finishing blow, really. Ask any hunter.
A warped fungus on a stick is a hunter's last friend. Shove it in a hoglin's face and it bolts the other way. I've never needed it. I always carry it. That's why.
We never take mothers with young. Hunter's law. Also because mothers hit harder.
The first bite goes to whoever carries the kill home. No carrier, no first bite. Even Brutes follow this. Even Brutes carry.
A ghast's scream will empty a whole forest of hoglins in one breath. A long creep through the trees, ruined. I shoot back. It doesn't help. It feels nice.

lines.text: My first kill was a small hoglin and I cried. Not for the hoglin. My bolt hit a stump and the hoglin walked into my knee. I cried for my knee. Don't repeat that.
I'll show you the best crimson stand someday. Three big old males and a mud-hole they all roll in. Mine since I was young. I trust you with it.
If you ever hunt with me, you carry the crossbow and I carry the shouting. Nobody has ever carried my crossbow. Except you, now. Sort of. Don't drop it.
Walking about with no gold in the crimson wood? Bold. Stay behind me, then. Hoglins don't care what you wear. Only what you smell like.
Fresh hoglin tracks! Big ones. Quiet now. Do you want to follow?

replies.text: Good. Step where I step. Breathe when I breathe. If I sneeze, run.
Hm! A careful one. Fine. Stay behind me. I'll tell the story later and put you in the front.
They ARE! That's the point! Why hunt a gentle thing? Where's the story in a gentle thing?

lines.text: Be honest. Could you hunt?

replies.text: Loud is good! Loud keeps the Rotted away. Loud is terrible for hoglins. Stay home.
They all say that. Bring a stick, a plan and a spare pair of knees.

lines: A crossbow, thirty bolts, a coil of cord, a warped-fungus stick, a skinning knife and a bag for tusks. Everything else is boasting.
Bolts get stolen by lava. Drop one over the edge and it's gone. I shoot with my back to the shore now. That cost me nine bolts and a boot.
The bowstring is hoglin sinew, twisted and waxed with fat from the last kill. It stinks. The stink keeps it strong. Good stink.
The cord is for hauling a kill out of a tight place. Hoglin in a gully, me above it. Tie it, haul it, argue about whose shoulders it ends up on.
I count tusks. My own, I mean. I won't say how many. More than the Brutes have axes. More than {neighbour}, who counts wrong.
Rival hunters are my favourite folk to hate. The ones from the next Hold hunt on our fungus, shoot our hoglins, then lie about the size. Their tales are always too small.
I'd never hunt in the warped canopy. Weft nets would hang me up like a smoked haunch. I'd rather meet a charging hoglin. At least he's honest.
I learned from Brakka Long-Eye. She could hit a hoglin's eye across a lava channel. She had one ear. The hoglin who took the other was the only one she ever missed.
Thick soles for hot ground, hide inside for the soft parts. My boots are so old they've learned my feet. They don't like anybody else's.
Rule of the trail: never leave a wounded one. A hurt hoglin is a mean hoglin. A mean hoglin is the whole Hold's trouble. So you finish it, and you finish it quick.
We paint the {clan} mark on the crossbow stock. If a hunt goes wrong, they find the bow and know whose it was. The bow remembers, they say. The hunter forgets, mostly.
A bad hunter shoots too soon. A good hunter shoots on time. A great hunter lets somebody else shoot and takes the story.

lines.text: I almost shot a Ghastkin whelp once. Under a cliff it looked just like a ghast whelp. Then it looked at me. I put the bow down with shaking hands. Told no one. Now you.
I hunt less now than I did. Not from tiredness. From care. Careful hunters grow old. Old hunters get to tell the tale as long as they like.
When the trees stop creaking, you're not alone. Something's watching. Don't shout. Walk back the way you came. I learned that from a scar. It's on my back. Don't ask.
Let me see your hands. You've never held a bow. Am I right?

replies.text: Honest! Rare! Hold it like this. Gently. It's alive in a nasty way.
Then show me. Not on me. At that stump. No, a farther stump. Further.
Hm. More hoglin for me, then. I'll try not to be hurt.

lines.text: Hunters have a toast. 'Full bag, full belly, empty trail behind.' Say it with me.

replies.text: ...EMPTY TRAIL BEHIND! HA! You've got the voice. Loud enough for a hunter.
Pass? On a toast? Fine. More for me.

lines: Smell first, eyes second, hands last. Crimson fungus smells like hot iron. Warped smells sharp and sweet, like a cut stem. Wart smells like old gold. Quartz smells of nothing, which is how you know.
The good shroomlights hang high where nobody reaches. That's why they're good. Easy ones are small and sour. I pick the hard ones and boast about them for ages.
A hooked pole, a net bag and a sharp knife. The pole snags, the bag carries, the knife argues with anything that bites.
Wart grows on soul sand, dry and red and ugly. You don't pick it for beauty. You pick it for the mash. A feast without mash is only a meal.
Quartz is the white vein in the black rock. Tap it with the knife handle. A clear ring is good quartz. A dull thud is a rock pretending. Rocks pretend a lot.
Never pick a fungus that glows wrong. Too bright, too green, too sweet-smelling. The forest is no friend. It's a patient neighbour with a bad temper.
Nether sprouts are for children and fools. Nice to chew, useless to sell. I chew them for luck. I need a lot of luck.
You don't pull the roots. You take the cap. Roots stay, cap grows back. Pull the roots and the forest goes bare, and then there's no work. Idiots forage once. Wise Piglins forage forever.
Twisting vines grow up and weeping vines hang down. Foragers climb both. Weeping vines make better rope, twisting vines hold more weight. Learn the difference or learn it falling.
Leave the wart blocks at the lava's edge alone. Lovely to look at, mean to touch. Nine foragers, nine burnt fingers. Ask me my count.
Rule of the pole: whoever's pole touches a shroomlight first owns it. Sharp elbows are allowed. {neighbour} has the sharpest.

lines.text: I keep one fine shroomlight in my bag that I never sell. Orange as a hearth. When the forest goes dim and my torch runs low, it's my little hearth. Don't laugh.
Foragers sing as they work. Not for joy. So the others can tell where we are if a floor gives out. I sing badly on purpose. That way nobody mistakes me for a hoglin in trouble.
My best find: a quartz seam the size of a longhouse door, behind a lava fall. I never told the Hold. I told you. Treat it kindly. Don't dig it all.
No gold, and you walked all the way out to my patch? Sit. Share my fungus. Friends eat the first cap, even the ugly ones.

lines: The forager's rule: look up, look down, look behind. Everything good and everything dangerous is in one of those. Mostly behind.

lines.text: Sniff this. Hold still, don't look at it. Crimson fungus or warped?

replies.text: Hot iron smell, yes! You have a nose. Keep it away from the hoglin pens or they'll bite it.
Warped! Sweet and sharp. Lucky guess, or a good nose. Either way, don't wave it near a hoglin.
Nothing? Then it's quartz. Or you've lost your nose. Check your nose.

lines.text: You'll carry for me? Take the heavy sack. Heavy means rich.

replies.text: Good. Don't drop it. It's mostly fungus, but there's one egg-shaped rock I love.
Ha! Lazy and honest. I can't hate that. Move on.

lines: The warped canopy holds the best shroomlights. It also holds the Weft. Getting one without the other is the whole art. I've done it twice. Both times I ran.
A Weft net drops with a click. Not a thud. A click. Then you're hanging, and a Weft is looking at you, patient as a stone. Awful. Awful.
Never climb a stem with a spool-line on it. Spool-lines mean a lookout. Climb a clean stem. Clean stems are slow. Slow beats netted.
Cut a net with a hot knife. Warm it on a lantern first. Cold blades skid. Mine has been through eleven nets. I should be ashamed. I'm proud.
I never take from a stem near a Loom. Not because I'm good. Because they remember faces. Their cloth remembers faces. I'd end up woven in as a villain.
A shroomlight comes off its stem with a wet pop. The Weft hear it. Pop, click, net. That's the song of my work.
Ever watched a Weft climb? Four arms. They don't climb a stem, they flow up it. I think about that when I'm trying to sleep.
Warped wart blocks are soft and bounce back. Step wrong and you bounce into the next tree. I once bounced into a sleeping Weft. We both apologised. Then he netted me. Fair.
Don't trust the canopy bridges. The Weft built them to hold Weft. A Piglin on a Weft bridge is a Piglin on a very long swing.
Shroomlights light up my home. A pole with one on top is a lantern that never goes out. Ask a Hold without a forager how bright their halls are. Dim. Real dim.

lines.text: I left a shroomlight on a stem once, a gift, no reason. Next time I came, a spool of thread lay in its place. Didn't touch it. Didn't trust it. Still think about it.
My brother Gruk went up after a big shroomlight and the Weft netted him. In the end they let him go, with a patch sewn on his belt. A neat patch. He's still angry how neat.
Between us, the shroomlights aren't worth the nets. We could trade. But gold means nothing to the Weft, so we'd need something else. I'm still thinking. Don't tell the Hold I'm thinking.
If I smell wet bark and old string, I stop and drop flat on my belly. A good forager knows how to be a stone. A great forager knows when to be a stone with a very good excuse.

lines: Foragers and Hunters fight about whose forest it is. It's nobody's. It's the forest's. But I get the first pick. Rule of the pole.

lines.text: Would you climb a Weft stem for a shroomlight? Honest answer.

replies.text: Easily, he says. Wait until you hear the click. Then tell me 'easily'.
Wise. I'd say that too, if I weren't so greedy. Greed is a wonderful way to get netted.
With me? Then we both hang. Good company, though. I'd tell jokes the whole time.

lines.text: I could use a second pole. Want to learn the canopy rules?

replies.text: Rule one: don't scream. Rule two: don't scream louder. Rule three: if you scream, scream at the Weft, not at me.
Watching is how I got my scars. From watching other people do things. Ha. Good plan.

lines: Gold ore is speckled stone. Gilded blackstone is the richer kind, if you can stand to dig it. Break it small, feed the furnace, and shout while it cooks. Shouting helps. Ask anyone.
A furnace has a voice. Low roar means too cold. High whine means too hot. A steady hum means perfect. I can hear mine from the far side of the Hold. So can everyone.
Bellows first, then fuel. Never fuel first. Fuel without wind just smoulders and sulks. Wind without fuel is only noise.
A good ingot pours smooth and sets with a shine. A bad one comes out crusted. We call that a sulk. Melt it again and it sulks less.
Gold sweats before it melts: a bead on the lip of the crucible, glowing. That bead is your signal to step back. Fools step in.
Slag is what's left over, dull grey crumbs. I keep a pile. The Goldsmith says it's useless. Then he comes back for it every few sleeps.
A leather apron, thick gloves, a rag round the face. That's the kit. The rag is for the smell. The smell is for my pride.
Magma cream goes in last, a pinch, and the pour runs sweet. Only the best Smelters know. Now you do. Don't ask where I get it.
The Magmari melt gold just by touching it. They do it by accident. I watched one walk off crying. Think what I could do with a hand like that.
A pour takes a count of forty. Count short and you pour short. Pour short and the Goldsmith shouts. I count loudly. He shouts louder.
Stand upwind of the pour. The fumes smell sweet and sing in your ears. Stay long enough and you agree with everything. I once agreed to lend a Brute my axe.

lines.text: I once lost a gold cap off my own tooth. It fell in. Wouldn't leave. Came out a tiny ingot. I wear it on a cord. The smallest ingot in the Hold, and mine.
A furnace must never go out. If it dies, the Smelter lights it again from the Hoard's hearth, in front of everyone, carrying the coal in bare hands. I'd rather lose an arm. I keep it fed.
I name every furnace. This one's Old Gullet. It ate my brother's boots. He swears it was an accident. It was a very hungry accident.
No gold on you? Friends don't need it here. Stand closer to the fire than the rest. A pour is about to come out, and you'll want to see it.

lines: Furnace ash goes on the paths. Slippery for a Brute, soft for a hoglin. I like to see it. Proof that I worked.

lines.text: Hold this ladle. No, the other end. The OTHER end! There. Feel the heat?

replies.text: Hot! Yes! Hot is the whole point. If it weren't hot, it'd be a Goldsmith's problem.
Can't feel it? Your gold must be thicker than your skin. Ha! Good gold.
Too late, you hold it now. Hold it like a friend. Nine breaths. Steady. There! You've smelted.

lines.text: Could you tend a furnace? Think carefully.

replies.text: Everyone learns quickly at a furnace. It teaches with fire. Fast teacher, that.
Honest. Smart. Stay a safe arm's length behind the rope. Further. There.

lines: Accident? Ha! Show me a Smelter without a scar and I'll show you a liar with a cold furnace.
My worst was a dropped crucible. A whole pour ran across the floor like a river and the Hold chased it with spoons. We got most back. Most.
Never pour into a cold mould. Cold bites hot. The ingot cracks, the mould cracks, the Smelter cracks. Warm the mould first. Sing to it if you like.
Ore with a hollow in it spits like a ghast when it heats. Tap every lump first. A dull knock means a hollow. I learned by being spat on.
The smoke turns blue when something's wrong. Blue means the fuel's wrong, or the ore's wrong, or I am. Always start by blaming the ore.
The Goldsmith says my ingots are too soft, too hard, too shiny, too dull, too heavy, too light. I smile. I have the bigger hammer.
Rival Smelters are the best kind. The one in the next Hold swears his ingots shine brighter. They don't. They're just yellower. Honest gold glows a warm red-brown. Mine do.
A Wanderer once asked for my furnace ash. I gave it free. He sold it as lucky ash from the finest forge in the Nether. I still can't decide whether to be flattered or hunt him.
Old Burnt-Brow Mudge taught me. He's retired to a bench by the horn tower now, where he shouts advice at my back. The advice is usually about twenty years too late.
Never smelt angry. Angry Smelters pour fast. Fast pours splash. Splashes sting. A calm Smelter is a rich Smelter with all his skin.

lines.text: I lost a thumb to a pour once. The Goldsmith made me a gold one. It's the finest thumb in the Hold. I wave it at people. Some wave back. Some run.
The worst thing isn't the burn. It's the ore that lies. Stone that glitters like gold and isn't. We call it sulk-stone. I've wasted whole furnaces on it.
When a new furnace gives its first good ingot, we keep that ingot. It goes into the wall. Mine's in the third course of bricks on the left. Shall I show you?

lines: Soot gets everywhere: under my nails, in my tusks, in my dreams. I dream in black and orange. Smelters' families all do.
A furnace that roars on its own is thinking about you. Don't ask why. Run, then ask.

lines.text: Be honest. Have you ever burned something badly?

replies.text: Good! Then you know fire. The ones who say never are the ones I keep away from my furnace.
Never?! Then you've never cooked anything either. Sad life. Pity.
A dinner burner! You'd make a fine Smelter's helper. We burn everything. Dinners especially.

lines.text: What's the one rule of fire?

replies.text: Wrong! That's the rule for Brutes. The rule for Smelters is: touch it, but once.
Respect! Yes! Fire respects those who respect it. It also eats them. But politely.

lines: Heat it till it blushes. Beat it till it sings. Cool it slowly or it sulks. Do that nine hundred times and you have a helmet. Nine hundred and one for the dents.
Gold is the softest metal and the proudest. Soft means it takes any shape you like. Proud means it remembers every blow. Hit it gently, or it will show every mistake.
Tongs, hammers, a stake, a pot of ash and a rag. The rest is patience. I'm out of the rest.
I fold the plate like a leaf. Heat, fold, beat, again. Nine folds make it strong without making it stiff. Eleven make it stiff. Fourteen make it snap. Nine.
A rivet is a promise. One loose rivet and a helmet comes off in a brawl and its owner is a bare-headed fool. I check every rivet three times. Three.
A gold edge on a plate of iron fools the eye and the Hold. It's honest enough. Gold is gold, even a thin line. Just don't call it armour. Call it a decision.
Every plate I make gets a clan mark on the inside. If a Piglin falls, we know whose he was. If he sells it, we know whose he was. Both are useful.
Polishing is where Goldsmiths go wrong. Rub too hard and the plate thins. Then it dents when you sneeze. I polish with ash and a thumb. A thumb knows when to stop.
Good gold sings when you tap it. A low clear ring, like a horn a long way off. A flat sound means a flaw. I tap everything. People think I'm nervous.
A helmet should fit like an argument: close, firm and impossible to take off. I measure heads with my hands. Brutes have the biggest. Children have the loudest.
Gold cracks if you bend it back and forth too often. So don't change your mind. Change your hammer.

lines.text: My teacher Grubba Fine-Hand could beat a plate so thin the light came through. She said any fool can make armour. A master makes armour that looks like nothing and stops a tusk.
Between us? I hide a tiny mark in every piece, a little snout no bigger than a grain. When I'm gone they'll find it and say 'That was him.' Now you know. Don't tell the Hold.
I'm making something for you. Don't ask. Don't look. It isn't done. It might never be done. A good gift takes its own time. I've been measuring you with my eyes since we met. Your shoulders lie.
No gold on you and you still came to the forge? Then you're no buyer. You're company. Sit by the bellows. Tell me what the Overworld smiths do wrong.
See this helmet? Be honest. What's wrong with it?

replies.text: Liar! There's always something. But I like the lie. I'll find the flaw myself and cry about it in private.
Sharp eye. That dent is a story. Or a mistake. For now, a story.
UGLY! It's practical! Ugly is practical's smaller cousin! Out of my forge!

lines.text: You wear gold. Who made yours? Don't lie. I'll know by the rivets.

replies.text: Obviously. Which one? Never mind. The rivets are sloppy. Show me, I'll fix them for free. Don't tell my clan I fixed them for free.
YOU made it? Then you're a Goldsmith too. Sit. Show me your hammer grip. No. Wrong. Like this.
Found it! Ha! Nobody just finds gold. Somebody lost it, died or got robbed. Don't tell me which.

lines: A good Goldsmith's hands are never clean. Soot, ash, glitter. The glitter is the worst. I find it in my meals. I eat it. Waste not.
Every Piglin in the Hold wears a piece of my work. Walking through a crowd is like seeing my children: loud, dented and sure they're the best.
The forge rule: you don't pay for the plate, you pay for the promise. If it fails you in a fight, I owe you a second. Free. It has happened twice. I'm still cross.
Apprentices carry ash and scrub tongs for a whole long while before they touch a hammer. They learn to listen first. The hammer teaches the rest.
I made a helmet for a Brute once. Took me forever. He grunted. I took it for thanks. Next time he brought me a hoglin haunch, all bone. That was thanks.
Rivals sharpen a craft. The Goldsmith in the next Hold makes plates with a shine you could comb your tusks in. Mine are better. Mine are just less shiny.
Now and then a Wanderer comes in with a bundle of old gold: broken helmets, bent rings, melted lumps. Each one has a story. I turn them into something new and the story stays inside.
I never throw away a dent. When a plate comes home battered, I keep the biggest dent flat on a shelf. If I lose heart I look at the shelf. They all came back.
Learning gold is learning patience. Piglins are bad at patience. That's why I'm good at it. I had to be bad at being a Piglin first.
The old Bastion smiths could draw gold wire so fine it hung in the air. Nobody can now. I try. I get a mess. A beautiful mess, but a mess.
Most want gold to look rich. I want gold to look hard. Rich gold sits there. Hard gold stops a tusk. Ask yourself which you'd rather be wearing in a fight.
A forge fire is lit once. If it ever goes out, the whole Hold feels it, down in the stomach. I've tended ours since I was small and it hasn't dared yet.

lines.text: I made my own armour first, as a youth. Awful. Looked like a sad bucket. I still wear it under the good one. It reminds me what beginners do.
Between us, the hardest work isn't armour. It's the clan rings. When one of the {clan} dies, I melt their favourite thing into a ring for the family. Gold carries them. That's honest work.
I put a tiny pocket of air in every rivet, a secret. In a fight it rings, faintly. I like to think the armour sings for whoever is wearing it.

lines: People ask which armour is best. The one you're wearing when you win. That one.

lines.text: I could use a hand at the anvil. Do you hit things well?

replies.text: Prove it. Hit that. No, not my thumb. THAT. Good. Again. Softer. You hit like a Brute.
Everything breaks eventually. Break the cheap thing first. That's the apprentice rule.

lines.text: Which would you rather have: armour that shines, or armour that holds?

replies.text: Both! Greedy! I like you. Impossible, but I like you. I'll try.
A practical one. Rare in a gold-wearer. Rarer in a friend. Keep that head.
Shines! Ha! A true Piglin. Sometimes a shine saves a life too. Mostly it loses one. But it's a lovely loss.

topics.ask: How do you keep a herd?
lines: Crimson fungus in, warped fungus far away, and never turn your back on the big one. Wait. Never turn your back on any of them. That's the whole secret.
Every pen has a head hoglin. The head decides who eats first. I learned to ask the head, not the herder. The herder agrees with the head. So does everyone.
Feed in a circle, never in a line. A line starts a fight at the end. A circle starts a fight in the middle. The middle is where I'm not standing.
Watch the ears. Ears forward, hungry. Ears flat, angry. Ears twitching, bored. Ears twitching and tusks low: run.
The pen gate has three bars and a rope. Hoglins can lift two bars. Nobody has beaten the rope yet. I tie it with a knot only I know. Even I forget sometimes.
I sing to the herd. Low, long, off-key. Hoglins don't like pretty singing. They like the sound of something big and sad and slow. Like me.
A calf is born with its tusks half in. It bites everything it can reach, including its mother, including me. I keep a leather mitt for calves. The mitt has a lot of holes.
I name most of them after the first thing they eat. Fungus, Pebble, Boot. Boot ate a boot. Pebble ate a pebble. Fungus ate fungus. It's disappointing. The real troublemakers earn proper names.
Keep them away from the portals. Anything that goes through comes back Rotted. Mad, green and sorry for its own tusks. I built a rope fence for that. They hate the rope.
Hunters bring me wild calves now and then. They bite worse than penned ones. But they grow big. A wild calf is a gamble. Gold likes a gamble.
Never run in the pen. Running says 'prey'. Walk like you own it. Walk like you owe it nothing. Walk like you could cook it, but won't. It senses that.

lines.text: I sleep in the pen when a mother's due. The warm breath of a whole herd is the best fire there is. Not the best smell. The best fire.
When a hoglin dies, I sit with it. I don't know why. Hoglins don't sit with each other. But somebody should. Don't tell the Hold I do it. They'd say I'm soft.
My best hoglin, Old Lump, is blind in one eye and deaf in one ear. He still leads the herd. I'm half like that. The other half is hungry.
No gold on you and the herd still lets you near? They smell friend on you. Hoglins can't tell gold from rust. They tell friend from food. Stay friend.

lines: The smell of the pen takes years to get used to. I'm on year nine. I've stopped noticing. Visitors notice. I find it flattering.

lines.text: Come closer. The herd smells you. Do you want to scratch the big one?

replies.text: Behind the ear, quick. Don't stop or he sulks. Don't go on too long or he thinks you're his. Both are trouble.
That's his friendly face. His real face you'd have heard about already.
Wise! I wouldn't either. I'm only brave when somebody's watching.

lines.text: Fifty hoglins, one herder. How do you think I manage?

replies.text: Skill, yes. Also a lot of running. And a very good fence. And a fear so deep it looks like respect.
Luck! Yes! Luck and a very good fence. Don't tell the fence.

topics.ask: What goes wrong in a herd?
lines: Sickness comes as a cough. A hoglin that coughs is a hoglin going down. I pen it apart, feed it crimson cap, sing. Half live. Half I'd rather not talk about.
Raiders. Not Weft or Magmari. Piglins from the next Hold, after our calves. Custom says you may steal a calf if you're quick and brave. So I'm quick, and I bite.
The worst sound in a Hold is a gate swinging. I check every latch three times. Then I check it again after I've checked it.
The Hunters think my herd is meat waiting to happen. I think the Hunters are hoglin-bait with crossbows. We're polite at the longhouse table. Never at the pen.
A hoglin that won't eat has a worry. I once found a nugget stuck in a tusk. Took it out, and he ate like a Brute. Gold is a worry, even for hoglins.
Calves learn to charge by hitting me. I don't recommend it. I recommend a pad. I wear one on my backside and one on my pride.
I pick which hoglin goes to the fire. It's the worst part of the job. I always pick the oldest, never the weakest. Respect first, meat after.
The Rotted wander near the pens sometimes. They don't hurt the hoglins. They just stand and stare. The hoglins stare back. A very long staring match. Nobody wins.
A hoglin that goes through a portal comes back mad and green. We call it a Rotted herd, even if it's just the one. It bites everything and dies of confusion. I've seen two. I want no third.
Never let blue fire near the pen. One soul lantern and the whole herd slams into the far wall, shaking. No Withren lanterns on this side of my fence. Not even polite ones.

lines.text: My teacher Mawla Soft-Hand could calm a herd by humming. I tried. They laughed. Hoglins laugh like a bellows. I'm still practising.
I lost the whole herd once to a ghast scream. They stampeded over the ridge. I found forty-nine in a gully and the last one wedged in a fungus cap, furious. Don't ask how.
If I ever leave the pen, you're the one I'd hand the rope to. You don't flinch when they glare. That's all it takes. Not skill. Not luck. Not flinching.
When a calf is born I give it a nugget to chew, for luck. It never swallows it. It never gives it back, either. Half the calves in the Hold have a nugget hidden somewhere. I've stopped looking.

lines: My three rules: never feed from your bare hand, never sleep with your boots on, never trust a quiet hoglin. A quiet hoglin is planning.

lines.text: A hoglin and a Hunter walk into my pen. Who do I help?

replies.text: Right. The Hunter knew the risk. The hoglin only knew lunch.
The Hunter?! He brought a crossbow into MY pen! Out!
Both! Brave. Foolish. Good. You'd make a herder. Mind the teeth.

lines.text: Would you keep a hoglin, if I gave you one?

replies.text: Then you'd learn. Keep it fed, keep it far from warped fungus, and don't take its tusks to bed.
Wise. Hoglins are for those who like to be needed. And bitten.

lines: Cold truth: I love them. Every bitey, stinking, stubborn one. Don't repeat that. They'd think I'm soft. They'd be right.
Stand. Watch. Don't sit. Sitting is how thieves win.
Watch the hands. Not the face. Faces lie. Hands steal.
The gate has one rule: gold or leave. The vault has no rule. The vault has me.
Hear steps from three bridges off. Good ears. Big ears. Laughed at once. Not twice.
Thieves come quiet, or loud and stupid. Loud ones are easy. Quiet ones keep me awake. Hrm.
I count the stones in the arch. Four hundred and nine. Four hundred and ten, if you count the cracked one. I count the cracked one.
Axe at my side. Hand near the axe. Never on the gate. Gate is stone. Stone doesn't need a hand.
One horn means come. Two horns mean thief. Three horns mean everything. Heard three once. Don't want to again.
Piglins bring me food. I don't ask. They don't say why. We understand each other.
Eat standing. Sleep standing. Dream of nothing. Best way to dream.
Some Piglins fear me. Some love me. I like both. Fear and love both stay out of the vault.

lines.text: I hum when it's quiet. Low. Don't tell. A Brute that hums is a Brute that's bored. Bored Brutes get ideas.
Counted the vault gold once. Every nugget. One short. Looked for it a long while. It was in my boot. Felt shame. Told no one. Told you.
You I'd let past. Not the vault. Past me. For a Brute that's a lot. For me that's everything.
No gold on you. Fine. Know your face. Stand near the gate while I watch. Nobody asks questions of a Brute's friend.

lines: A thief ran from me once. Lava took him. I stood a long time. Hrm. Not a good thing. Don't want to talk about it.

lines.text: Hrm. Come near the gate. Go on.

replies.text: Hrm. Closer. Stop. That's near enough. Good. Now you know where near enough is.
Hrm. Smart. Most are.
Hrm. Want to see?

lines.text: Hrm. One question. Ask.

replies.text: Hrm. When the gate rests.
Hrm. Lonely? Gate is company. Axe is company. You're company. A little.

lines: Axe. Name's Thunk. Dumb name. Mine.
Heavy. Heavier than you. Carry it a long walk. Then talk.
Handle of crimson stem, wrapped in hoglin hide. Hide gets worn. Hide gets changed. I don't complain.
The Brute's oath: guard until the gold is gone or I am. Gold's not gone. I'm still here.
Brutes are picked young. Smallest, angriest. Trained with a wooden axe. Wooden axe hurts too.
First swing I broke a bench. Second I broke a thumb. Third I broke nothing. Hrm. Third was hard.
Axe doesn't lie. Axe doesn't talk. Axe doesn't haggle. Good friend.
Nobody else lifts it. Not allowed. Not wanted.
I fight slow. Slow means I choose. Fast means they choose.
Brutes aren't born mean. Taught mean. Then mean stays. Then we stand at gates.
Sharpen with basalt. Slow strokes. Same count each side. Fifty. A Brute who skips the count is a Brute who misses.

lines.text: Axe has a notch, here. First thief. The notch stays. I look at it when I'm unsure.
A small one tried to steal it once. Hands too small. Dropped it on his foot. I carried him to the Goldsmith. Axe touched nothing else that whole sleep. Hrm.
When I'm done, the axe goes to the next Brute. With the notch. With the name. Thunk. Hrm. You may hold it. Once.
There was a Brute before me at this post. Never met him. His axe-marks are on the doorframe. I add mine under his. Someone adds under mine.
Hrm. Want to lift it?

replies.text: Hrm. Careful. Both hands. Knees bent... Good. You lifted. Don't tell anyone. Or tell everyone.
Hrm. Wise.
Hrm. Nothing too big. Only you too small.

lines.text: Hrm. You swung an axe before?

replies.text: Hrm. Show me. Not at me.
Hrm. Start with wood. Always wood.

topics.ask: What's it like in a ruin?
lines: You learn the floor first. Which stones hold, which stones lie. A newcomer gets a lump of chalk and a funny walk. By his second sleep he walks like us, or he falls.
We patch with whatever we find: blackstone, bricks, gold plates off old doors. Our walls are the richest in the Nether. Patchwork rich.
The housing halls are the warmest. The stable halls are the loudest, because the old troughs make everything echo. The bridge is the windiest. Hot wind up from the lava, always.
The children play on the bridge and we pretend not to watch. A fall is a lesson, and the lava is a hard teacher. I'd rather they learned it from a bench.
Sweep the ash and find gold. Sweep the gold and find more ash. It's the best job in the Nether and I'm not sure why.
We cook in the old kitchens, black-bricked and huge. Pots the size of a Brute. I stir with a plank. It takes three Piglins and one shout to lift a lid.
Shout 'Gold!' in the old treasure hall and the room answers 'Gold, gold, gold.' I do it when I'm sad. The room always agrees with me.
Every wall has a name. The Singing Wall, because it hums when the hot wind is right. The Sulky Wall, which keeps cracking. The Brave Wall, which stood when the fire came.
Hold folk think we're backward. We think they're shallow. They live in crimson wood that never burns. We live in stone that already did. Ours has seen the worst. Theirs is guessing.
Beds are rare. We sleep in heaps on the warm stones, one pile of Piglins to a room. Thirty snorers, one big breath. Safest sound in the Nether.
Visitors ask where we got the carved doors. We found them. Where? Behind that wall. How did we know? We listened. Doors know when they want to be found.

lines.text: Each sleep we count everyone in the Bastion out loud. We were many once. We count the few that are left, loudly, so the dead can hear we're still here.
At the heart of the Bastion there's a hall with no roof. The roof fell in the fire. We never rebuilt it. The lava glow fills it all the way up. We swear our oaths there.
I found my mother's name scratched on a beam in the housing hall. She wrote it when she was small. I never knew she could write. I leave it. I polish around it.
Nobody sleeps in the north hall. Not because of ghosts. Because of the draught and the smell. Also ghosts.
Gold or no gold, a friend gets a warm room. Take the one by the stair. It's the only one the fire forgot completely. Don't mention the bell.
Do you like ruins, outsider?

replies.text: You do? Then you'll like this one. The best ones have been burned a little. Like us.
Sad? Maybe. But sad stones and loud Piglins, that balances out.
Rebuild! With what? With whom? We keep it the way the fire left it. A scar tells the truth.

lines.text: Want to stay a while? We have rooms. Mostly floors.

replies.text: Welcome! Don't touch the third step, don't lean on the Sulky Wall, and don't ask about the bell.
Go! Come back with gold. Don't come back with questions about the bell.

lines: Everything. Old plates, door hinges, gold melted into twisted shapes, bits of bone, the odd tooth. Nothing is thrown out. Everything is weighed.
The best finds are the gold runs: places where the fire melted the gold and it ran into cracks and cooled. You chisel them out. A run the size of a hand is a feast.
A pry bar, a chisel, a sack and a rope. The rope matters most. A floor you dig through can give way. The rope is the only friend that won't argue back.
Soot hides everything. Scrub a patch and look. If the stone is red, the fire was hot and the gold ran. If it's grey, the fire only sulked. Dig the red.
Never dig under the old stable hall. The troughs are heavy and the floor is thin. We lost a good digger there. We named the trough after him. Not as a compliment.
A found helmet goes to the Goldsmith, a found hinge to the Smelter, a found bone back into the wall. We don't take bones from the dead. Old custom. The Weft do, I hear. Pah.
{neighbour} once found a chest of nuggets under a staircase. We sat round it for a count of ninety without touching it. Then we shared it. Then we argued about the sharing. Normal.
I found a chipped bell once. Small. Rang once. The whole Bastion went quiet. We hung it by the roofless hall. It rings on its own when the hot wind is right. That's the bell.
The treasure halls still have traps: old pressure stones, blocked doors, bad floors. I don't open a vault door. I tap it, listen, and tell a Brute. Brutes love opening doors.
They say there's a door in the lowest hall that nobody can open. Flat, black, no handle. I knocked once. Something knocked back. I haven't gone down since.
Digging is slow. You learn to talk to the stone. 'Come on, give us a nugget.' It gives you a nail. 'Come on, give us a nugget.' A hinge. In the end: a nugget. Patience pays.

lines.text: I take one thing from every dig and put it on my shelf. A hinge, a nail, a charred spoon. A Bastion of little things. Mine is the only keepsake-shelf in the Nether.
I found a child's toy once, a gold hoglin the size of my thumb. It has teeth marks. I carry it. It's no use. It's the best thing I own.
If you ever want to dig the old vaults with us, I'd put your name forward. The Brutes wouldn't like it. The Brutes like nothing. But I'd say it.

lines: The Wither melted a lot, but not all. Somewhere the gold is still where it was, sealed in the dark, unburned. A whole room of gold, untouched. I want to find it more than I want to eat.

lines.text: Think there's anything left worth finding?

replies.text: The right answer. If you stop thinking there's more, you stop digging, and then you're just standing in a ruin.
Hmph. That's what quitters say. Quitters sit by the fire and wonder where the gold went.

lines.text: Hold my rope. If I yell, pull. If I laugh, don't.

replies.text: Good. If the floor gives, I yell. If I find something, I laugh. If I do both, pull harder.
Everything good is. That's the price of having something to tell.

lines: News costs a nugget. Good news costs two. Bad news is free, but you pay later. I carry it in my head, not on a scroll. Scrolls burn.
A Wanderer's first rule: tell each Hold what it wants to hear. Second rule: remember who wanted to hear what. Third rule: remember who to avoid next time.
I know every Hold's quarrels. Who owes whom a hoglin. Which Goldsmith stole whose rivet. It makes me rich two ways: nuggets and gossip. Gossip lasts longer.
I shout my news at the gate before I enter. The Brute listens, nods, lets me in. With no news I'd be a stranger. News makes me a guest.
Lying cost me once. I told a Hold their rivals had gone into the lava. They hadn't. They came through the gate shouting. I have never run faster, or lied bigger.
The loudest news is who won the last brawl. The quietest is who lost. The valuable is who got bribed. Sell all three, each differently.
I carry one small gift for every Hold: a nugget, a fungus, a bone. I hand it over at the gate and say the Hold's name. They never forget. It's worth ten ingots of friendship.
Some Holds pay me to carry news away. 'Say nothing about our ring.' Others pay me to bring it. Same news. Different pockets.
The Rotted never ask for news. Best listeners in the Nether. They stand there and don't interrupt. I tell them everything. They tell nobody.
Children love me. I tell them what's in the next Hold. They gasp. They think I'm a hero. I let them. Heroes eat first.
News travels slower than I do. That's the only reason I have a job. A faster news would put me out of work.
Careful what you say near me. I repeat everything. Not to hurt anyone. I just can't keep a thing in. I'd make a poor Brute.

lines.text: Truth: sometimes I carry no news at all. I just walk. The gate Brute nods, I nod back. We both pretend I'm important. It's a good game. It's most of the job.
I once carried a message from a dying Piglin to his daughter in the next Hold. Four bridges, a lava fall and a Weft net. I'd do it again. I didn't take the nugget.
I'll tell you which Holds fib about their size, which are in trouble, and which have the best roast. I tell very few. You're one of the few now.
No gold on you? Then you've learned the last Wanderer rule: carry your welcome in your face, not your pockets. Every Hold knows my face. Stay with me and they'll learn yours.
Got news for me? Fair swap. A nugget for a tale.

replies.text: Good. Here's your tale: the Brute at the next Hold sneezed so hard he fell off the horn tower. Lived. Angry.
No news? Then you're bad at living. Go make some. Come back and tell me.
A lie! I love a lie. As long as it's good. Go on. Make it a big one.

lines.text: Want me to carry a word for you? To anyone, any Hold. First word is free.

replies.text: Done. 'The shiny one comes.' They'll hide the good roast. Or hide the bad roast. We'll see.
Hm. A secret-keeper. My least favourite kind. Fine. Not a word. Out loud.

lines: The road between Holds is mostly lava with a little bridge in it. The bridges are older than the Holds. Nobody knows who laid them. Everyone walks them and nobody asks.
Count your steps on a new road. If the count's different on the way back, you've been walking on something that moves. Get off.
Rule of the cairn: stack a stone, leave a nugget. The next Wanderer takes the nugget and adds a stone. The cairn grows. So does the road. We're odd about our roads.
Sleep on your gold. Truly. If it's under you, you wake when it moves. If it's in a bag, you wake when it's gone.
Soul sand is a trap. Slow and sticky. Walk around, never through. Unless a Withren is watching. Then walk through and look brave.
Never follow a lone light off the road. Lights out there are blazes, or lanterns, or worse. I follow my own nose and my own gold.
A fallen bridge isn't the end. It's a chance to climb. Crossing a broken span with a rope in your teeth is how I got these arms.
I know where the ghasts drift in a line, one after another, always crying. I walk under them with a hand on my crossbow and a hum in my throat. They hate humming.
There are roadside shelters: blackstone huts with no doors, a stack of fungus to burn, a slab to sleep on. Whoever built them was kind. Whoever uses them leaves a nugget.
Weft nets across the road mean turn back. Withren lanterns across the road mean a Vigil is near. Magmari chains across the road mean pay a toll. Piglin horns mean run.
Every Hold smells different from the road. Crimson smoke, hot metal, hoglin dung. I can name a Hold blind by the third whiff. Hold folk hate hearing it. I mean it kindly.

lines.text: I've been lost three times. Each time I found a Hold I'd never heard of. Each time I told no one. Each Hold is my secret. Don't ask about them.
A Wanderer's worst fear isn't the Rotted. It's a road that ends: a bridge that goes nowhere, a stair that stops. The next step is lava. I always check the next step.
If I don't come back from a walk, tell them I was last at the cairn by the basalt bend. Leave a nugget. They'll know. That's enough.
Friends of mine don't need gold on the road. Walk beside me and the cairn-keepers wave you through. A Wanderer's friend is a Wanderer's guest. Even bare.
Walk the road with me for a while? You'll learn more than you ask.

replies.text: Good. Keep your gold on and your mouth shut when the ghasts scream. Mine stays open. Mine's the loud one.
Slow is how you live long on a road. I'll slow down. A little. For you.
Pah. Safe at the hearth. Enjoy your hearth.

lines.text: Which would you rather meet on a lonely road: a Weft, a Magmari or a Withren?

replies.text: You'll be haggled to death. A fine way to go. Bring snacks.
Brave. They'll say your name sadly and you'll hear it for a long time.
A Weft? Then you'll be hanging by the ankle before your next breath. Click click. Lovely.

lines: Let's play Barter! You're the ring and I'm the Piglin. Give me an ingot. I admire it. One, two, three, four, five, six. Here's a stick!
Hunters is the best! I'm the hunter and {neighbour} is the hoglin. They have to run on all fours and snort. They never snort right.
Forge! You hit a rock with a smaller rock and shout 'Shiny!' Then the Goldsmith shouts at you. The Goldsmith is a real grown-up and means it.
In Herder you're a hoglin and you bite. I'm the herder. I get bitten. I always cry first. The rules say the herder cries first.
Brute is the hardest. You stand still and don't blink. First to blink loses a nugget. I lose a lot of nuggets.
Wanderer is a running game. You run to the next bench with a message and shout it really loud. Then the other person shouts it back wrong.
When we play Bastion we jump the cracks! Don't fall in the crack! Falling means you're Rotted and have to walk slow and say 'uhhhh'.
I'm always the Smelter. I don't need eyebrows. I draw them on after. Grown-ups say it's cheating. I say it's art.
No real gold in games. Real gold goes on the pile. Pretend gold is a stone. Mine is the shiniest stone. I licked it to make it shinier.
I won Barter once by saying 'your gold is cursed.' They gave me everything. I felt bad. A bit. Then I ate the everything.
If you play Hunters with us you have to be the hoglin. You're big. You're good at being scary.
Our games are better than the grown-ups' jobs. In ours nobody gets burned.

lines.text: You can be the Bartermaster. You're the best at pretend shouting. Hold up the ingot and say 'Hmm.' Like you're thinking. Hmm! That's it!
Secret: I play Brute alone sometimes, when nobody looks. I stand by the gate and don't blink. I never got past forty. A real Brute walked by once and patted my head.
When I'm big, can we play for real? You be the Wanderer and I'll be the Hoard. No, YOU be the Hoard! I'll guard you and you can't leave!
You're not shiny but you can still play. Grown-ups say gold is for working. Games don't need gold. Games need friends.
Pick a game! Barter, Hunters, Forge, Herder or Brute?

replies.text: Yes! I'll be the ring! Give me the ingot! ...It's a pebble. It's fine. It's a very good pebble.
Hunters! You're the hoglin! Run! Snort! SNORT! No, not like that, like a hoglin!
Brute! Don't blink! Don't blink! ...You blinked! I win! Pay me a nugget!
Tired? You're a grown-up. All grown-ups are tired. Sit. I'll bring you a pebble.

lines.text: Who always wins at your games?

replies.text: Yes! Always! Except when {neighbour} cheats. They cheat a lot. They cheat with their feet.
Nobody wins! That's the BEST way to play. Then nobody cries. ...Then somebody cries.

lines: I carry fungus for the Forager! Two at a time! Three if nobody's looking. I dropped four once and the Forager yelled in a very interesting voice.
I'm not allowed near the furnace. I'm allowed to look from behind the rope. I look so hard my eyes get hot.
At the pens I scoop the dung. It's the worst job. It's also the most important job. The herder said so. Then he gave me a bigger scoop.
I hold the tongs at the forge! Well, I hold them while they're cold. The Goldsmith says someday they'll be hot. I'm not sure I want that.
The Bartermaster lets me say 'Next!' at the ring. I say it really loud. Sometimes nobody's waiting. I say it anyway.
I polish helmets! You put ash on and rub and rub. My arm falls off. Not really. But it feels like it did.
I fetch things for the Hunters. 'Fetch the string!' I fetch. 'Not THAT string!' I fetch another. There are lots of strings.
When the horn blows I have to run to the longhouse and hide under the bench. That's my job in an emergency. Somebody has to be under there.
I clean tusks! Well, after they're cleaned, I check them by chewing. Somebody has to.
A Wanderer gave me a message to carry across the Hold. I forgot it on the way. I told them everything I could remember instead. It was mostly about hoglins. They said that was probably right.
Grown-ups give me one nugget for a big job. I've saved twelve. I hide them somewhere different every time. Even I forget.
I tried to help the Brute. He said 'Hrm.' I think that means yes. I carried his axe. For two steps.

lines.text: Sometimes the grown-ups let me dig in the old ash pile for gold. I found a button! A gold button! They said it belonged to someone. I said it belongs to me now.
I want to help more, but the grown-ups say I'm small. I say small is useful. Small gets under things. Small found the lost tongs.
Secret: I do the best job in the Hold and nobody knows. I check the gate latch every time. Every single time. Nobody asked me. I just do it.
My favourite is when the whole Hold is working and loud and I'm in the middle. Everyone's busy. I'm busy. We're busy together. It feels like gold.
Want to help me carry something? It's heavy. Fine, it's light. Fine, it's a pebble.

replies.text: Yes! You carry the pebble! I'll carry the shouting. I'm best at the shouting.
Aww. Fine. I'll carry it myself. Slowly. So you feel bad.

lines.text: Grown-ups say a helping hand is better than gold. Is it?

replies.text: Hmm! Even better than gold? Hmmm! I'll think about it. Gold is very shiny.
I KNEW it! I'm telling everybody you said that! They'll hate it!

lines: The Bartermaster shouts at gold until it gives him a present. I want to shout at gold too. Nobody lets me. I'll shout at a nugget when nobody's looking.
The Hunter hides in the trees, jumps out and shouts. I know that's not exactly it. But that's what I saw.
The Forager climbs up and gets lights. Sometimes the Weft get him. He comes home all tied up in string and shouts at the string.
The Smelter has no eyebrows because he ate them. Mother said. She winked, so I think it isn't true. Or it is. She winks at everything.
The Goldsmith hits gold until it's shy. Then it goes on a Piglin. Then the Piglin is shiny and the gold is happy. That's how it works.
The herder smells like hoglin because he IS a hoglin. A hoglin in a Piglin suit. I haven't proved it yet. I'm collecting proof.
The Brute never moves, so I thought he was a statue of a Brute. But he blinks. A really slow blink. I timed it. I counted to three hundred.
Wanderers walk and walk and walk. I think they're running away from something. Or looking for lunch. Or both.
Bastion folk live in a broken house and think it's the best house. I live in a good house and think it's boring. We should swap.
Grown-ups talk about work all the time. 'My work, my work, my work.' I think it's a game with lots of rules and no winning.
Brutes are born angry because they got hit by the horn. A horn is big. I'd be angry too.
Grown-ups argue about whose job is hardest. Hunters say theirs. Herders say theirs. The Smelter says nobody else is on fire. That one wins.

lines.text: I asked the Goldsmith how he knows the gold is ready. He said 'it tells me.' I put my ear on a nugget. It said nothing. Maybe it's shy.
When I'm big I'm going to do ALL the jobs. One after another. Then I'll be the richest Piglin who never had any time.
Grown-ups say they're tired. But then they laugh and shout. I think tired is a game too. I'm very good at the tired game.
My favourite grown-up is whoever gives me a nugget. Right now it's the Smelter. Last time it was the Hunter. You could be next. That was a hint.
Which job is the best? Pick one!

replies.text: Bartermaster! Because of the shouting? Me too! Shouting is a very good job. I want it when I'm big.
Hunter! Ha! You get to be scary and eat the thing you were scary at!
Goldsmith! Because of the shiny? Yes! Shiny is the best reason for anything.
Brute?! You like the angry big ones? I like them too. But from far. Far, far.

lines.text: Do you have a job? A proper one?

replies.text: Ooooh! Like a Wanderer who hits things! That's the best job. Better than all the others put together!
Me too! We can decide together. You decide first. Then I'll do the opposite and win.

lines.text: When two Piglins meet, we clack tusks and shout our clans. Whoever's clan is shouted loudest buys the first mug.
Never count another Piglin's gold out loud. It's rude. Count it quietly, in your head, and be jealous in private.
A guest at the hearth pays one nugget at the door. Door-nugget. It buys the warm end of the longhouse and a bowl of whatever's boiling.
Every deal starts with a bite. Real gold gives a little under the tooth. A cheat's gold makes you spit.
Never whistle near the Hoard. Whistling is how thieves call each other. Ask any Brute. Then duck.
Shake with the gold hand, never the weapon hand. A weapon-hand shake is a duel. Offer it only if you mean it.
The last bite of every meal goes to the pens. Hoglins remember who feeds them. They also remember who doesn't.
A crossbow passed over empty is a present. Passed over loaded, it's a promise. Either way, say thank you.
Owe a Piglin gold and you wear a strip of red fungus on your belt till it's paid. Look at {neighbour}'s belt sometime.
We name hoglins after cousins we can't stand. Then we feed them well, and that's as close as a family gets to peace.
Sleep with your feet to the door and your gold under your head. Thieves and in-laws both come through the door.
Lose a tusk in a fair fight and the winner stands you a mug of mash. Sore tusks need company.
Horn blows twice: drop everything and count heads. Horn blows once: drop everything and eat. Don't mix them up.
In the barter ring the buyer shouts first and the seller shouts last. Mumbling costs one nugget.
Between friends I let you win one argument. One. Don't waste it on something small.
A friend may borrow my second-best helmet. Never my best. A best helmet is part of a Piglin. You don't lend a nose.
Bastion manners: step over the cracks the fire left, never on them. We keep every crack. They're the oldest decorations we've got.
I leave a nugget under a flat stone at every camp. The next wanderer takes it and leaves two. Well. One. Fine, one.
A hunter never names the kill till it's skinned. Bad luck. Ask me again when it's on the spit.
The first ring out of any new pour goes into the forge fire. For luck. Also it's always lumpy.
Greet every hoglin by name at the gate, even the new ones. They don't know their names yet. Say it loud till they do.
Custom. Stand. Stare. Do not sit.
Brutes don't share hearths. Share walls. Good enough.
Salute is axe-butt on the floor. Once. Twice is a challenge.
Do your folk greet with tusks, fists or a nod? Show me how you'd do it.

replies.text: Ha! Louder! A name that nobody hears is a name that gets stolen.
A NOD? Like a sleepy hoglin? Fix that. Shout something. Anything.
Hands! Good. Which one? Gold hand or weapon hand? Careful what you say.

lines.text: The Great Count! Once a litter or so the whole Hold hauls the Hoard out, counts it, and hauls it back. Whoever loses count buys the mash. Nobody finishes counting. Nobody finishes standing.
The Long Shout: we line up on the edge of a lava sea and bellow across it. Loudest voice wins a gold ring. The ghasts always answer, so we call it a tie with them.
The Gilding is for the young. Your first armour from the Hold's own forge, and you get dusted with gold flakes from tusk to toe. You sneeze gold for a long while.
Every thousandth ingot out of the furnace is a Thousand Feast. Three hoglins on the spit, the Hoard doors open, and the babies may touch the gold. Once. Quickly.
Tusk-Clash is our wrestling: two Piglins, one ring, no axes. First to lose a tusk is the loser. If both lose one, it's called a friendship.
The Hoglin Run! They open the pens and every young Piglin sprints ahead of the herd. Whoever's still in front at the far fungus gets the first cut of the roast.
A new litter gets a naming feast. We lay each baby on a hide with a nugget in each fist, and whoever holds on longest earns the loudest name.
At the Founding Feast we light the first fire in a new longhouse. Everyone brings a log and a boast. The log goes on the fire. The boast goes on forever.
The Ring-Fair opens the barter ring to every trade, no questions, no hitting till the third horn. After the fourth horn, hitting is welcome.
We feast when a hunt goes well, when a hunt goes badly, when a hunt is cancelled, and when nobody remembers the hunt. It keeps us busy.
The Stomp: everybody in a circle, stamping, tusks clacking, until the floor gives. It's not dancing. Dancing is for the Weft, who have the arms. This is stomping with feeling.
We cook in the old Bastion kitchen once every Count. The roof's gone, so the smoke goes straight up, and the ghasts come to look. We wave a drumstick at them.
At a hunter's feast the one who took the beast sits at the head and tells it three ways. The three ways must not match. Matching means you're lying.
At the Gilding I dust the babies myself. It's the only time I'm allowed to waste gold. I waste it with joy.
Somebody always asks the Smelter to light the big furnace for show. Last time I singed the roof. They cheered. They asked again.
The Ring-Fair is my feast! Everybody gets to be me for a little while. They're all terrible at it.
I follow the feasts from Hold to Hold. They're all loud, they all run out of mash, and they all feed a Wanderer. I never go hungry.
The herd gets a feast too. Crimson fungus piled to the rafters and no Piglin allowed in the pens till they've finished. They'd eat us otherwise.
Forager's feast: all the fungus we can carry, laid on one hide. Roasted, raw, rolled in ash. Not the warped kind. Never the warped kind.
Stand next to me at the next Count and I'll show you how to lose count with dignity.
Come to the Founding Feast and sit with my clan. Guests of honour get the heel of the roast and a great deal of shouting.
Feast. Brute guards the roast. Nobody steals. Brute eats the crumbs.
Brutes don't dance. Brutes stand near the dancing.
Count. Hoard Brute counts first. Nobody checks.
What do you celebrate in your world? Say something loud.

replies.text: You count YEARS? We count gold. Same thing, only mine gets heavier.
NOW you're talking! Do you have a ring? You need a ring.
Sitting quietly. A feast of nothing. Sad. We'll fix that. Bring your family.

topics.ask: What do you like to eat?

lines.text: Hoglin! Roast it, fry it, stew it, pickle it in ash. Every part but the squeal. We'd eat the squeal too if we could catch it.
Crackling is the best of the hoglin: skin crisped on a hot stone till it sings. Whoever's nearest the stone gets the first piece. Fights are common.
Gilded crackling is for feasts, dusted with scrapings from the goldsmith's floor. Gold on food does nothing for the taste. It does everything for the boast.
Wart-mash is our drink: nether wart pounded, soured in a hide sack, drunk the moment it fizzes. It smells like a Withren's feet, I'm told. I've only heard.
Crimson fungus roasted on a flat stone until the cap curls. Good for the belly and the temper. Not good enough for the temper.
We never eat warped fungus. It sours the pens, sours the mood and puts the hoglins off their feed. Eat it and you'll be asked to leave. Through a wall.
Quartz is for chewing, not swallowing. We rub it on our tusks to make them white. The whitest tusks in the Hold are called Bright Mouths and they're very smug.
Rotted flesh isn't food, it's an insult. Offer a Piglin rotten flesh and prepare to be punched.
Black pudding is hoglin blood stirred with ash and fat, boiled in a gut. It looks like coal. It tastes like coal that's been loved.
Don't ask what's in the barter-ring stew. The Bartermaster will tell you and you'll regret it. It's tasty, though. Mostly.
A feast portion has rules: the heel to the eldest, the tail to the youngest, the middle fought over. That's how we learn about fairness.
Children get crimson caps rolled in hot fat and left to crisp. They crunch. The crunch is half the fun. The other half is stealing them.
The old Bastion kitchens still have the great spits. Bent by the fire. Roast on a bent spit and the meat comes out curved. We call it the bastion bend.
My mother's stew was hoglin shank, fungus, ash and a loud word to the pot. Nobody makes it like she did. Mine tastes like an argument.
When you visit, you get the best seat and the best bone. Not the second-best. The best. Don't tell {neighbour}.
Dried hoglin strips are what I carry on the road. Hard as a boot, tasty as a boot. Lasts through any war.
A wanderer eats cold. Fire draws the Rotted and thieves. I haven't had a hot meal in ages. I'm very tough. And very hungry.
We smelters cook on the furnace ledge: whatever fits in a hide bag, left in the heat till it swells. Eyebrows optional.
I eat standing, with a spoon of pure gold. Soft metal, so the spoon's always bent. A bent spoon is the sign of an honest meal.
I don't eat hoglin from my own pens. Mine have names. Names are the difference between a meal and a neighbour.
Roast-wart cakes! Pound the wart with ash and fat, flatten on a hot stone. Chew for a long time. You'll hate them, then you'll want another.
Meat. Raw is fine.
Eat last. Eat most.
Fungus is for hoglins. Brute eats meat.
What do Overworld folk eat? Don't say grass.

replies.text: PORK?! You eat pork too?! We have more in common than I thought. Bring me some. Cooked.
Vegetables. Is that a kind of fungus? You eat green things? Poor, poor Pink-skin.
Bread! Apples! Are they gold? They're not gold. Pity. But I'll try one. Just the one.

lines.text: Gold is the one friend who gets heavier the longer you keep him.
Never lend a boot you can't shout across the Hold to get back.
A closed fist keeps gold. An open fist keeps friends. Everyone has two fists. Use both.
Never trust a quiet Piglin. Never trust a loud one either. But the loud one tells you where he is.
Boasting is just truth that hasn't happened yet.
He who bites the nugget first tastes the lie first.
Every Hoard starts with one pebble rubbed on a nugget. Don't laugh at pebbles.
Lava is patient. Piglins aren't. That's why there are more of us in the lava than you'd think.
A tusk lost in a fair fight grows back wiser. A tusk lost in an unfair one grows back angry.
If you can hear the Rotted, you're too close. If you can't, you're too late.
A nugget that lands edge-up means a quarrel. Flat means a fight. A nugget that doesn't land means a thief.
A ghast shrieks in your left ear: bad luck. In your right ear: someone's coming for your boots. In both: sit down.
A hoglin that turns three times before lying down will have young. A Piglin who does it has an itch.
Wear your helmet to the ring and take it off at the hearth. Do it the other way round and the gold sulks.
Never count your gold in front of a Weft. They'll weave the number into that Cloth and the whole Nether will know.
Spit on a new axe before you swing it and it bites where you point.
A soft Piglin is just a hard Piglin who hasn't been hit yet.
Gold in the purse, hole in the purse. Gold in the Hoard, hole in nothing.
When the fire spits blue, put your tusks away.
A friend is somebody who's seen you lose a fight and still says you won.
Never sleep near a Brute who's hungry. Brutes are always hungry.
Sing before a hunt and the hoglin hears you coming. Shout after, and it won't hear anything again.
Gate shut. Gold safe. That's the saying.
Hit first. Talk after.
Gold drops, you pick it up. Omen.
Say a saying of your own. Make it loud, make it short, make it mean something.

replies.text: None! Then borrow mine, I've spares. Say it with me: shout first, count later. Good. Now you're wise.
Wise, and short. Keep that one. Poke nothing you can't eat.
True! Cheerful, too! We'll get along, you and I.

topics.ask: Want to hear of my world?

lines.text: Your world! The rotting one! Is it true the roof is blue and too far to touch? Who stops it falling on you?
Tell me about the sun. I heard it's a gold block rolling across the sky and nobody guards it. Nobody! Why hasn't someone taken it?
I heard water falls out of your sky on purpose. Doesn't it put out your fire? How do you cook?
Grass! A whole floor of it! Is it fungus? Do you eat it? Do your cows? I heard your hoglins are called cows.
Your beds don't explode? Not even one? You lie down in them on purpose? That's braver than any Brute.
The Rotted go back and forth through your portals. You must keep a whole house for them. Do you feed them? Do you even know their names?
Green creatures that creep up and blow themselves apart? That's a ghast on legs. I'd put one on a banner.
I heard Overworld folk trade with green stones. Green! Not gold! Who would swap a good ingot for a green stone?
Your villagers hum at each other. Hmm. Hmm. That's the whole bargain, I heard. Terrible bargainers. I'd take them to the ring.
Iron men guarding the villages! Giant, grey, with flowers in their hands. Flowers! Do you sing to them? I'd like to fight one. Briefly.
Your sky has a pale rock that rolls round after the gold block leaves. That's when the Rotted come out. Which proves everything I've said.
You've no tusks? How do you eat? How do you win arguments?
When you're hurt, do you bleed gold? No? That's sad. Do you at least bleed something shiny?
If you live in the rotting world and you're not rotting, you're hiding something. A strong helmet. A secret ingot.
If I went through the portal with you, would I rot at once or slowly? Slowly? How slowly? Never mind. I'll stay here. For now.
I want to see your sun, once. From the portal. Just the edge of it. With an axe in hand and a full belly.
You've seen the sky. I haven't. Describe it using only things I know. No, not lava. Try again.
Do they keep hoglins in your world? Cows, you say? Are they fat? Do they bite? What a useless animal.
Do they work gold in your world, or only iron? Say they work gold. Say it's pretty. I'll weep.
They keep wolves in the house, I heard. Feed them bones. Call them friends. In the HOUSE. I'd love to see a tame one hunt.
Is your fire as loud as mine? Don't lie. Tell me your furnaces roar.
I've walked every road in the wastes and they all end at lava. Yours must be longer. Do yours ever end?
Overworld. Rot. Stay out.
You went. You came back. Brave. Or lucky.
Sun. Is it gold? Bring a piece.
What's the best thing in your world? Tell me true.

replies.text: Home! Yes! That's the best thing in anyone's world. Next you'll tell me it smells.
OBVIOUSLY! Finally someone from your rot-world with sense!
The sky. Hm. It's too far to bite. I don't trust anything I can't bite.

lines.text: My cousin Krunn shot a ghast whelp once that turned out to be a Ghastkin child. He felt bad. Brought it a nugget. It cried over the nugget. He asked for nothing like that.
My grandsire crossed a lava sea on a Magmari barge, back when they still took Piglins. The ferrywoman haggled the whole way. He got off owing three ingots and a boot. The family still owes.
A Weft measured my ear once, with a string. Then wrote the number down on that Cloth of theirs. Why does a Weft want my ear?
A Withren stood outside our gate and said nothing for a whole Count. We threw pebbles. It said, 'Thank you.' Never been so confused in my life. We left it alone.
They say a Ghastkin tear closes wounds and washes away memories. I'd never drink one. I might forget what I'm owed.
The Magmari can't hold gold at all. It melts on their skin. So what do they boast about? Chains? Imagine boasting about a chain.
The Withren carve every dead name in a wall. Imagine the carving. We shout the name once and move on. Shorter. Louder.
Weft have four arms. FOUR. They can hold a nugget, an axe, a cup and a grudge, all at once. It isn't fair.
A Ghastkin cried at the funeral of a Piglin it had never met. We didn't know whether to hit it or hug it. We did both.
I saw a Vigil once, from a ridge. Blue lanterns down every lane and not one voice in the place. I counted forty lanterns before I looked away first. Don't tell the Brutes.
None of them wear gold. Not one. Four peoples and not one has the sense.
The Withren call us loud. The Weft call us greedy. The Magmari call us thieves. The Ghastkin just look sad. I'd rather be called names.
Meet a Withren on the road and I draw. Meet a Magmari, I draw. Meet a Weft, I draw and look up. Meet a Ghastkin, and I'm not sure. It depends how sad it looks.
Between us, a Ghastkin healed my cousin's arm once. A tear on the wound, quick and cold. He was knocked out. He's been angry about it ever since.
I don't hate them all. I hate the idea of them. When one is in front of me I hate it less. It's a flaw. I'm working on it.
If you meet a Magmari who isn't cold, ask about her chain. They love that. Then warm her by the fire and she'll talk your ears off.
I tracked a Weft through the canopy once. It tracked me back. We shared a ledge and neither of us blinked, not once. I'm still not sure who won.
Foragers meet the Weft more than anyone. We fight over the same shroomlight. They're polite about it, which is the most annoying thing a person can be.
The Magmari chainwrights would never let me see them cast. They'd say my gold would melt. They'd be right. I'd still go.
I've crossed paths with all four. Withren: quiet. Magmari: loud and haggling. Weft: watching. Ghastkin: avoid, or you'll start crying too.
Not our kind. Kill? No. Watch.
Weft have four arms. Watch all four.
Withren bad. Magmari bad. Weft bad. Ghastkin sad.
Have you ever spoken to one of them? I mean really spoken?

replies.text: SEVERAL? And you still have your gold? Bold, or very charming. Which?
Good. Keep your tusks sharp and your questions short.
Not so bad! That's how it starts. First not so bad, then you're weeping with the Ghastkin.

topics.ask: How do you remember the war?

lines.text: I wasn't at the war. My grandsire was. He carried cook-pots for the war-bands. He says the smoke was so thick he served one stew to the same Piglin four times and nobody noticed.
Everyone's grandsire won the war. Every single one. Funny how we still lost the bastions.
My grandam stitched hoglin-hide helmet linings for the war-bands. She says every one came back with a different dent, and every dent had a name.
The Magmari ferried my grandsire's war-band across the lava. He was sick over the side of the strider. They charged him extra for the stain. He's still angry.
We sing the Nine Nuggets at the Count. It's about a Piglin who loses a nugget, then a friend, then a boot. It never ends, because the singer always forgets who's left.
The old tellers say the gold under the soul valleys glowed like a sleeping hoglin's belly. I'd have paid anything to see it. I'd have paid nothing, actually. Just taken it.
The tellers say the first gold helmet was a mistake. A smelter dropped a pour on his own head. He lived. He declared it a helmet.
My uncle says the war ended because both sides were too tired to shout. That's not true. We shouted the whole time. We just couldn't hear ourselves.
Old Gleamtusk was the first Piglin to wear gold. He dug an ingot out of the soul sand and wore it on his head. Everyone laughed. Then the war came. Now every clan says he was theirs.
The first Brutes were the ones who never went home from the line. They guarded the gates after the war and never really stopped.
Some of the old war-gold is cursed, they say. Soul-touched. It never warms in your hand. I'd take it anyway. I'd just wear gloves.
The war made the first good crossbows. Before that we threw things. Rocks, nuggets, relatives. The crossbow is the war's one good idea.
Our forge fire was carried from the old war-forge, hand to hand, and never let die. When the Smelters grumble, we say: the fire's older than your complaint.
Hoglins hauled carts in the war. My grandsire's pulled one through a lava ford and came out fine. The Piglin on top came out singed. The hoglin got a double ration. The Piglin got a lecture.
The bastions were the grandest places in the Nether. They say you could shout in one end and be answered from the other, a full count later. Now you shout and the wind answers.
After the fire we gathered whatever the gold left behind: a ladle, a crown with no jewels, a boot. They hang in our Hoard as the Nine Leftovers.
Some of the old ones said, let the Weft take the bones. A needle is a better ending than rotting. Most hit the one who said it.
The gold ran down the walls like lava, and for once nobody stooped to pick it up. That's how you know how bad it was.
My family was in the vault when it came. My grandam says the three heads said names, over and over. She never knew whose. Don't tell the Brutes.
We found a hall in the Remnant with the roof still on. We call it the Quiet Hall, because nobody has had the heart to shout in it. Not yet.
Every Remnant has one wall nobody rebuilds. Ours has handprints in soot. Small ones. Nobody says whose.
War. Long ago. Gate remains.
Brutes stood the line. Brutes stand it still.
Fire came. Gate stayed. Gate still here.
Would you have fought in the war, do you think? Be honest. Boast, but be honest.

replies.text: That's the spirit! Loud, certain, and no idea what's coming. A perfect recruit.
REFUSED?! Hm. You're either wise or a Magmari in disguise. Show me your hands.
Talk to three heads with no ears? We shouted at it. It didn't answer. Rude.

lines.text: My first nugget was a pebble. My mother rubbed it on a real one till it shone, and I wore it everywhere. I knew. I wore it anyway.
When my first milk-tusk fell out, it went into the longhouse fire for luck. The second went into my aunt's helmet. She's never found it. I check.
I learned to count on a hoglin's ribs. Left side up, right side down. Nobody ever reached a hundred. The hoglin kept moving.
My mother's cradle-song was the Count. She sang numbers until I slept. I still wake at forty-one.
First Barter: when you're old enough you must swap one thing for another with a stranger, alone, in the ring. I came home with a boot, a rock and a debt. Still not sure how.
We played Snatch in the pens and Horn on the roofs. I broke a tusk, an arm and my aunt's favourite pot. Not all in one game.
A baby hoglin bit me on the backside once. I wear the scar like a trophy. The trophy is on my backside. I can't show you without a fight.
I was too small for armour, so my parents hung a gold ring round my ankle and told everyone I wore a full set. Nobody believed them. I did.
My father taught me to shout from the belly, not the throat. 'Throats give out,' he said. 'Bellies keep going.' He was right. He's hoarse anyway.
My mother could fill a longhouse with one 'EAT!' I've never matched it. I'm still trying. Mostly I empty it with other words.
Every young Piglin dreams of being a Brute. Then they find out Brutes eat last. Dreams get smaller after that.
The Brute on the horn used to lean over and stare down at us. We froze. Now I'm grown, and I still freeze.
The elders said the Rotted come for children who don't finish their porkchops. I've never left a bone since.
We slept in a heap, litter on litter on hide. The middle was warmest, so we fought for the middle. I got it once. I was squashed. It was glorious.
I tracked {neighbour} for a whole stretch when I was small, thinking they were a hoglin. They were asleep. I was very proud of myself.
My mother put one nugget in my hand, said 'Keep it,' and left. She came back after a long while. I still had it. She said, 'Good. Now you're ready.'
They let me near the forge because I was too stubborn to be sent away. I still carry the scar from my first bellows.
I grew up in the pens. My first friend was a hoglin calf. It grew bigger than me and never forgave me for the nickname I gave it.
My first piece was a bent nail I called a ring. My aunt wore it to every feast. She said it was lovely. It was terrible. I love her.
My first deal: I swapped my own tooth for a nugget. Then the nugget for two teeth. Then I couldn't eat. Lessons.
